notes: Reading track definitions. Catholic canon: 46 OT books (1074 ch) including 7 deuterocanonical books, Esther with additions (16 ch) and Daniel with additions (14 ch), plus 27 NT books (260 ch).

flags.skimmable: Long stretches most first-time readers skip. Powers a core-chapters-only toggle.
flags.deferred: Placed late on purpose despite canonical position.
flags.deuterocanonical: Not present in Protestant Bibles. Useful if you ever add a canon setting.

tracks.name: Story First
tracks.tagline: Follow the plot, fill in the rest after
tracks.tradeoff: Four books sit out of canonical position on purpose
tracks.why: Reads the narrative backbone as one continuous story, then drops the prophets, poetry and deuterocanon into the historical moment they belong to. Highest completion rate of any approach because you are never stuck in one genre for long.

phases.name: Prophets of the Divided Kingdom
phases.note: These men were shouting during 2 Kings. Read them here and they finally make sense.

phases.name: Exile
phases.note: Tobit is a family story set among the deported. It is the human scale of the exile.

phases.name: Wisdom and Worship
phases.note: The inner life of the people whose history you just read

phases.name: The Silent Years
phases.note: The 400-year gap. Where the Pharisees, Hanukkah and the Roman occupation come from.

phases.name: The Deep Cuts
phases.note: Now you have the framework. Hebrews only makes sense against Leviticus.

tracks.name: Chronological
tracks.tagline: Events in the order they happened
tracks.best_for: History lovers who want a strict timeline
tracks.tradeoff: Still hits Leviticus and Numbers early, and some placements are debated
tracks.why: Arranges every book by when its events occur rather than by genre. Job is placed first on the traditional reading that it is set in the patriarchal age, though many scholars date its composition to the Persian period.

tracks.name: Classic
tracks.tagline: Genesis to Malachi, exactly as printed
tracks.best_for: Disciplined readers who want the traditional arrangement
tracks.tradeoff: Lowest completion rate. Most people stall in Leviticus or Numbers.
tracks.why: The order printed in Catholic Bibles: Pentateuch, Historical, Wisdom, Prophets.

tracks.name: Story First
tracks.tagline: Meet Jesus fast, then watch the church spread
tracks.tradeoff: Gospels are not in canonical order
tracks.why: Opens with the shortest gospel so you get a win in week one, keeps Luke and Acts together as the single two-volume work their author wrote, and saves Revelation for last because it is built almost entirely out of quotations from books you will have already read.

phases.name: Paul's Letters
phases.note: Roughly in the order he wrote them, so you watch his thinking develop

phases.name: The End
phases.note: Read it first and it is noise. Read it last and it is a summation.

tracks.name: As It Was Written
tracks.tagline: In the order the documents were actually composed
tracks.best_for: Readers curious about how Christianity actually developed
tracks.tradeoff: You read letters about Jesus before you read the story of Jesus. Some dates are contested.
tracks.why: The New Testament was not written in the order it is printed. Paul wrote decades before the gospels were finished. This order shows you what the earliest churches knew and when.

tracks.name: Classic
tracks.tagline: Matthew to Revelation, exactly as printed
tracks.best_for: Readers who want the traditional arrangement
tracks.tradeoff: Four gospels back to back means reading the same story four times before anything moves forward
tracks.why: The order every printed Bible uses: gospels, Acts, Paul by descending length, general letters, Revelation.

tracks.name: The Full Arc
tracks.tagline: One continuous story, opening with a hook
tracks.best_for: Almost everyone reading the whole Bible for the first time
tracks.tradeoff: Mark is split from the other three gospels, and four books are held to the end
tracks.why: Opens with the shortest gospel so you meet the main character in week one, then goes back to the beginning and runs the whole story forward. Maccabees sits right before the gospels so the 400-year gap is filled in rather than skipped.

tracks.name: Daily Mix
tracks.tagline: A bit of everything, every day
tracks.best_for: People who want the whole Bible in a year and burn out on one genre
tracks.tradeoff: You jump between eras every day, so you lose the sense of continuous story
tracks.why: Runs four parallel streams at once. Variety prevents burnout because you are never stuck in a difficult section for more than a few minutes. Widely considered the most sustainable long-term approach.

streams.name: Psalm of the day
streams.note: Psalms also appears inside the OT stream. Because progress is journaled globally by book and chapter, reading it here credits it there too.

streams.name: Proverb of the day
streams.note: 31 chapters, one per day of the month, loops forever.

tracks.name: Classic
tracks.tagline: Genesis to Revelation, cover to cover
tracks.best_for: Disciplined readers, or a second time through
tracks.tradeoff: Highest dropout rate of any approach. It takes months to reach the gospels.
tracks.why: The traditional arrangement. Simple to follow and requires no planning, but it puts you in ceremonial law and genealogies before you have built any momentum.

tracks.name: Timeline
tracks.tagline: Every event in the order it happened
tracks.best_for: History lovers, or a second pass through the Bible
tracks.tradeoff: Jesus does not appear until roughly 80 percent through, and some placements are debated
tracks.why: All 73 books arranged by when their events occur. Best for cause and effect across generations, weakest as a first read because the payoff comes so late.
